title: General Equilibrium Effects of Cash Transfers: Experimental Evidence from Kenya
summary: This study uses a large-scale randomized controlled trial in rural Kenya to measure the aggregate economic impacts of unconditional cash transfers. The authors find that transfers generate significant positive spillovers for non-recipient households and local firms, resulting in a local transfer multiplier of approximately 2.5 with minimal price inflation.

title: No Household Left Behind: Afghanistan Targeting the Ultra Poor Impact Evaluation
summary: This paper evaluates the impact of the 'Targeting the Ultra Poor' (TUP) program in Afghanistan, a multi-faceted intervention providing livestock assets, cash stipends, training, and coaching to extremely poor households. The study finds that the program significantly increased consumption, assets, and psychological well-being, while reducing poverty and indebtedness, suggesting that 'big-push' interventions can be effective even in fragile, conflict-affected settings.

title: Business Case and Intervention Summary: Hunger Safety Net Programme Phase 2 (HSNP 2)
summary: This document outlines the business case for the second phase of Kenya's Hunger Safety Net Programme (HSNP 2), which aims to provide predictable electronic cash transfers to the poorest households in arid and semi-arid lands. It details the program's strategy to integrate with the National Safety Net Programme, build government capacity for sustainable financing, and establish a scalable mechanism for emergency drought response.

title: The Hunger Safety Net Programme (HSNP) Phase 2 Project Completion Review
summary: This document is a project completion review of the Hunger Safety Net Programme (HSNP) Phase 2 in Kenya, which provided unconditional cash transfers to vulnerable households in arid and semi-arid lands. It evaluates the programme's performance, achievements, and challenges, including issues with dormant accounts, payment agent malpractice, and the transition to government ownership.

title: Understanding Factors to Evaluation Uptake: A User Centered Approach to Adapting Evaluations and Learnings
summary: This document explores the International Rescue Committee's efforts to improve the uptake of emergency response evaluations by adopting a user-centered, iterative approach. It analyzes three distinct evaluation methodologies—Emergency Response Reviews, After Action Reviews, and Hybrid approaches—to identify barriers to implementation and strategies for increasing the relevance and actionability of findings.

title: Comparing Robust Decision-Making and Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways for model-based decision support under deep uncertainty
summary: This paper compares two model-based approaches for decision-making under deep uncertainty: Robust Decision-Making (RDM) and Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways (DAPP). By applying both methods to a hypothetical river management case in the Netherlands, the authors demonstrate that the approaches are complementary, with RDM excelling at identifying vulnerabilities and DAPP providing a structured framework for adaptive planning over time.

title: Randomised Impact Evaluation in Humanitarian Action: A Learning Agenda for the Humanitarian Initiative
summary: This document outlines a learning agenda for integrating rigorous randomised impact evaluations into humanitarian programming, with a specific focus on protection outcomes. It identifies key research questions, addresses common implementation challenges in fragile settings, and proposes practical design strategies for humanitarian practitioners and researchers.

title: Insufficient Evidence? The quality and use of evidence in humanitarian action
summary: This study examines the challenges of generating and utilizing high-quality evidence within the international humanitarian system. It proposes six criteria for assessing evidence quality and analyzes how early warning, needs assessment, monitoring, and evaluation processes currently function to inform humanitarian policy and operations.

title: Evaluation of Humanitarian Innovation and Evidence Programme: Summative Phase Two
summary: This report provides a summative evaluation of the UK Department for International Development's (DFID) Humanitarian Innovation and Evidence Programme (HIEP). It assesses the programme's relevance, effectiveness, impact, and value for money, concluding that while HIEP successfully generated high-quality evidence and innovation, it faced challenges in translating this into systemic change and requires more proactive influencing strategies.

title: The Evidence Effect: Evidence for action in conflict and crisis
summary: This article discusses the role of randomized evaluations in humanitarian aid, highlighting how evidence-based research can improve the effectiveness of interventions in conflict and crisis settings. It reviews findings on the impact of cash transfers, empathy-building programs, and livelihood initiatives in supporting vulnerable populations and displaced communities.

title: Humanitarian impact evaluations: WFP and J-PAL build commitment for a common cause
summary: This article discusses the collaboration between the World Food Programme (WFP) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) to integrate rigorous impact evaluations, such as randomized controlled trials, into humanitarian aid. It highlights how evidence-based research can improve the effectiveness of interventions in crisis settings, ranging from cash transfers to anticipatory climate action.

title: The Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus
summary: This briefing examines the current state of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus, highlighting progress in coordination and policy reform alongside persistent challenges like siloed funding and limited local engagement. It evaluates the effectiveness of current nexus approaches in addressing protracted crises and identifies the need for clearer objectives, better measurement, and stronger integration of local actors.

title: IASC Discussion Paper: Exploring the linkages between AAP, Localisation and the HDP Nexus
summary: This discussion paper examines the systemic barriers to humanitarian reform and explores how integrating Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), localisation, and the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus can create a more people-centred aid architecture. It provides recommendations for decentralizing coordination, improving funding flexibility, and fostering complementarity to better meet the needs of crisis-affected communities.

title: Operationalizing the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus in Ukraine
summary: This case study examines UNDP's efforts to implement the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) Nexus in Ukraine, particularly following the 2022 full-scale invasion. It analyzes the challenges of siloed funding and coordination, while highlighting successful strategies for integrating recovery, resilience, and social cohesion into humanitarian response frameworks.

title: Breaking Boundaries: Local and National Actors’ Engagement in the Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus
summary: This report examines how local and national actors (LNAs) conceptualize and implement integrated humanitarian, development, and peace (HDP) nexus programming. It highlights that LNAs often adopt holistic, community-driven approaches that differ from international frameworks and provides recommendations for international actors to better support and fund these locally led initiatives.

title: Working across the humanitarian-development-peace nexus: What can we learn from evaluations?
summary: This paper synthesizes findings from 90 evaluations to assess how humanitarian, development, and peace actors are operationalizing the 'triple nexus' approach. It identifies persistent systemic barriers, such as siloed funding and a lack of operational guidance, while highlighting emerging good practices in coordination and context-specific programming.

title: The Triple Humanitarian, Development and Peace Nexus: In Context and Everyday Perspective
summary: This edited volume examines the operationalisation of the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus, exploring the tensions between theoretical frameworks and everyday practice in conflict-affected settings. It features diverse case studies and expert analyses that highlight the structural, political, and power-related challenges of integrating these three sectors to address the root causes of complex crises.

title: Humanitarian - Development - Peace Nexus Guidelines
summary: This document provides a comprehensive framework for implementing a 'nexus' approach, which integrates humanitarian, development, and peace actions to address the root causes of vulnerability and conflict. It offers practical guidance, checklists, and strategies for country teams and partners to improve coordination, joint planning, and adaptive programming in protracted crisis settings.

title: Faraway, So Close: Coupled Climate and Economic Dynamics in an Agent-based Integrated Assessment Model
summary: This paper introduces the Dystopian Schumpeter meeting Keynes (DSK) model, an agent-based integrated assessment framework that simulates the co-evolution of economic dynamics and climate change. By modeling heterogeneous agents and stochastic climate shocks, the authors demonstrate that climate change can lead to more severe economic damages and regime shifts than those projected by standard computable general equilibrium models.

title: Multi-level participation in integrative, systemic planning: The case of climate adaptation in Ghana
summary: This paper introduces the Multi-level Integrated Planning and Implementation (MIPI) process, a participatory methodology designed to bridge disconnects between local, district, regional, and national governance levels. By applying this process in Ghana, the authors demonstrate how diverse stakeholders can co-create systemic analyses and integrated plans to improve climate adaptation and food security.

title: Responding to climate services in the context of drought: A systematic review
summary: This systematic review synthesizes 88 journal articles to analyze how climate services (CS) influence the behavioral, perception, and attitude responses of users in the context of drought. The study finds that farmers primarily respond to CS by adjusting crop management, while non-farmers focus on policy and planning, and it highlights a need for shifting CS development toward better supporting user decision-making processes.

title: Risk without place: Why most climate risk assessments fail to support place-based adaptation
summary: This paper presents a systematic review of 86 global climate risk assessments to evaluate how spatial risk analysis is integrated into adaptation planning. The authors introduce the Spatial Risk Analysis Rubric (SRAR) to demonstrate that while hazard and exposure mapping are common, most assessments lack the depth in vulnerability and consequence modeling required for effective, equitable, and place-based climate adaptation.
